title: Planning and Recording Investigations
seo_title: JSS 1 Intermediate Science: Planning and Recording Investigations Worksheets (NERDC)
standard_code: JSS 1 Intermediate Science: Science and Development
standard_text: Students plan investigations by identifying and controlling variables, choose suitable equipment and units, record data accurately in tables and graphs, calculate means, and evaluate results and conclusions. (summary of the Intermediate Science curriculum, JSS 1, theme: Science and Development)
meta_desc: Free JSS 1 Intermediate Science worksheets (NERDC curriculum, theme: Science and Development): variables, fair tests, measuring and recording data, means, graphs and evaluating conclusions. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Change one variable, measure one variable, control the rest.
key_sub: Repeat trials and find the mean.
body_html:
How to think about it

An investigation begins with a testable question and a hypothesis. The independent variable is the one you change; the dependent variable is the one you measure; controlled variables are kept the same so the test is fair.

Record data in a table with units, repeat trials and calculate the mean, and plot a graph to see the pattern. Evaluate the results: are there outliers, errors or limits? Draw a conclusion that is supported by the data.

Example

Trials: 12 s, 14 s, 13 s. Mean?

Add and divide

Answer: 13 s

Example

Testing how salt amount affects boiling point. Independent variable?

What you change

Answer: the amount of salt

Common mistakes

  • Changing more than one variable at a time.
  • Leaving units out of a table.
  • Claiming more than the data show.

items.q: Investigation: “Does the length of a lever affect the force needed to lift a load?” Which variable should be changed?
c: the force needed to lift the load
the same load and the same pivot position
items.e: Change one variable: the one in the question.

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “The seedling in the cupboard was pale and 9 cm tall.”
c: a prediction made before the test
items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.

items.q: Investigation: “Does the amount of sunlight affect how tall a sunflower grows?” What should be measured?
c: the height of the sunflower after three weeks
the same seeds, soil, pot size and amount of water
items.e: Measure the result (the dependent variable).

items.q: A class investigates how the temperature of water affects how fast a stock cube dissolves. Which is the dependent variable (the one you measure)?
c: the same amount of water and the same kind of stock cube
items.e: Change: the temperature of the water. Measure: the time to dissolve. Keep the same: the same amount of water and the same kind of stock cube.

items.q: Investigation: “Does the material of a wrapping affect how fast an ice cube melts?” Which variable should be changed?

the same size of ice cube, the same thickness of wrapping and the same room

items.q: A class measured the time to boil for a volume of water in a kettle from 250 to 1,250 mL. Why is it risky to predict the result for 12,500 mL?

Larger values are always more accurate.

items.q: A student heats water in beakers of different sizes to test which stove heats fastest. Which change would best improve the investigation?

Read the scale at eye level.
items.e: The beaker size and amount of water were not controlled.

items.q: Which source is most reliable for a science report?

items.e: The conclusion is not supported by enough data.

items.e: Range = largest − smallest = 9.0 − 8.0 = 1.0 °C.

items.q: What does 'reproducible' mean?
c: other scientists get the same results when they repeat the method
items.e: Clear methods make results reproducible.
